sections.title: Part 1: The Hospital Mix-Up & Nan-Kaka's Discovery
sections.speech_ssml: <speak>Welcome to <emphasis level='strong'>My First Steps</emphasis> by Sunil Gavaskar! <mark name='story1'/> Born on July 10, 1949, Sunil was almost swapped at birth in the hospital! His uncle Narayan Masurekar, whom he called Nan-kaka, noticed a little hole on his left earlobe. The next day, the baby had no hole! After a frantic search, baby Sunil was found sleeping peacefully next to a fisherwoman.</speak>
sections.notes_content:
## Part 1: The Hospital Mix-Up

- Born July 10, 1949.
- Uncle Mr. Narayan Masurekar (Nan-kaka) observed a tiny hole near the top of his left ear lobe.
- Next day: baby in the crib had clean earlobes!
- Frantic search launched across hospital wards.
- Baby Sunil located sleeping peacefully beside a fisherwoman.
- Providence and Nan-kaka's eye saved Gavaskar's identity.
key_takeaways: Nan-kaka's observation of the earlobe hole prevented a lifelong mix-up
Sunil attributes his cricketing destiny to this providential discovery
Careful observation is established as a central theme of the text

sections.title: Part 2: Early Cricket Days with Mother & The Bleeding Nose
sections.speech_ssml: <speak>Now let us look at Sunil's earliest cricket matches! <mark name='cricket1'/> He played daily in the house gallery with his mother. One day, a straight drive hit his mother directly on the nose, causing it to bleed! Despite the pain, she washed her face and continued bowling, encouraging his dedication!</speak>
sections.notes_content:
## Part 2: Early Childhood Cricket

- Practiced with tennis balls inside the narrow gallery of his home.
- His mother bowled to him patiently every afternoon.
- A powerful straight drive struck his mother's nose, causing heavy bleeding.
- Demonstrating heroic composure, she stemmed the blood and insisted on continuing the game.
key_takeaways: Maternal dedication laid the psychological foundation for Gavaskar's sportsmanship
Relentless practice in confined spaces sharpened his straight-drive technique
Resilience under adversity was modeled by his mother

sections.title: Part 3: Intext Comprehension & Character Dynamics
sections.speech_ssml: <speak>Let us analyze the key figures in this autobiography. <mark name='traits1'/> Nan-kaka is eagle-eyed and vigilant. His mother is selfless and encouraging. Sunil is humble, passionate, and deeply grateful to his family.</speak>
sections.notes_content:
## Part 3: Character Analysis

- **Narayan Masurekar (Nan-kaka)**: Observant, decisive, caring relative.
- **Sunil's Mother**: Patient mentor, prioritized her son's passion over personal discomfort.
- **Tone of the Text**: Humorous, modest, rich in sensory detail and gratitude.
key_takeaways: Character traits are revealed through concrete actions rather than abstract assertions
Family mentors provide critical encouragement during early development
Prepare for 1 and 2 marker factual recall questions

sections.title: Part 1: Formation & Classification of Compound Words
sections.speech_ssml: <speak>Welcome to the Advanced Language Workshop! <mark name='comp1'/> A compound word joins two distinct words together to form a brand new meaning. Notice the three types: open compounds like 'gas stove', hyphenated compounds like 'eagle-eyed', and closed compounds like 'earlobe' and 'fisherwoman'!</speak>
sections.notes_content:
## Part 1: Compound Words

1. **Closed**: *earlobe, fisherwoman, newborn, courtyard, daydream*
2. **Hyphenated**: *eagle-eyed, right-handed, tennis-ball*
3. **Open**: *gas stove, bus stop, car park*

Each type acts as a single semantic unit.
key_takeaways: Compound words unite two words to create new, enriched vocabulary
Differentiate between closed, hyphenated, and open compound forms
Identify compound words in English literature passages

sections.title: Part 2: The Simple Past Tense & Irregular Past Verbs
sections.speech_ssml: <speak>Let us master the Simple Past Tense! <mark name='past1'/> Regular verbs add '-ed', but irregular verbs change their vowel structure completely. Gavaskar writes: 'Nan-kaka came', 'he saw', 'the baby did not have', and 'a frantic search began'.</speak>
sections.notes_content:
## Part 2: Simple Past Tense (V2)

- Used for actions completed at a specific time in the past.
- Regular: *noticed, played, washed, stemmed, continued*
- Irregular: *came, saw, gave, found, began, struck*
- Key rule: maintain past tense consistency across paragraphs.
key_takeaways: Autobiographical accounts depend on correct Simple Past conjugations
Identify irregular verbs that do not follow the standard '-ed' rule
Apply correct verb forms in narrative sentence construction

sections.title: Part 3: Past Habits: Using 'Used to' and 'Would'
sections.speech_ssml: <speak>How do we describe repeated past actions? <mark name='habit1'/> We use <emphasis level='strong'>used to</emphasis> and <emphasis level='strong'>would</emphasis>! Sunil 'used to play' tennis-ball cricket with his mother every afternoon. 'Used to' describes states or habits, while 'would' describes repeated past routines.</speak>
sections.notes_content:
## Part 3: Past Habits

- **Used to**: States or habits no longer true (*He used to play in the gallery*).
- **Would**: Repeated routine actions in past narratives (*His mother would bowl to him*).
- Always followed by the base infinitive form of the verb.
key_takeaways: Differentiate between one-time past events and habitual past routines
Construct sentences expressing past hobbies using 'used to' and 'would'
Recognize nuanced stylistic differences in narrative prose

sections.title: Part 4: Forming Negative & Interrogative Sentences with 'Did'
sections.speech_ssml: <speak>To ask questions or form negatives in the past: <mark name='did1'/> Always use <emphasis level='strong'>did</emphasis> with the base verb! Say: 'Did he notice the mark?' Never say 'Did he noticed'. The auxiliary 'did' already carries the past tense!</speak>
sections.notes_content:
## Part 4: Negative & Question Forms

- **Negative**: Subject + did not (didn't) + V1 (*He did not notice*).
- **Question**: Did + Subject + V1 (*Did he notice the baby?*).
- Golden Rule: Never pair 'did' with a V2 past-tense verb.
key_takeaways: The auxiliary verb 'did' carries the past tense mark
The lexical verb must revert to its uninflected base form
Practice error-correction for common grammatical examination traps

exam_questions.question: Explain the grammatical difference between 'used to' and the simple past tense, providing two examples based on Sunil Gavaskar's childhood.
exam_questions.answer_key: The simple past tense refers to completed actions at a specific time (e.g., 'He struck his mother on the nose on July 10'). In contrast, 'used to' expresses recurring habits or states in the past that are no longer true (e.g., 'He used to play tennis-ball cricket with his mother every afternoon').

sections.title: Part 1: Note-Making Principles & Structural Outlining
sections.speech_ssml: <speak>Welcome to Expert Tier! <mark name='notes1'/> Note-making is a vital academic skill taught in this chapter. Never write full sentences. Condense paragraphs into numbered headings, sub-headings, and standard abbreviations like 'e.g.', 'govt.', or 'deptt.'.</speak>
sections.notes_content:
## Part 1: Note-Making Mechanics

1. **Heading**: Central topic of passage.
2. **Sub-headings**: Secondary details indented.
3. **Points**: Brief phrases, not full sentences.
4. **Abbreviations**: Minimum 4 standard abbreviations.
5. **Key to Abbreviations**: Included at the end.
key_takeaways: Extract essential facts while eliminating extraneous grammatical filler
Maintain consistent decimal or alphanumeric indentation
Essential skill for high marks in board English examinations

sections.speech_ssml: <speak>Let us analyze the family influence on Sunil's growth. <mark name='family1'/> His mother gave him dedication and basic practice. His father gave him technical advice. His uncle Madhav Mantri taught him the moral lesson: there are no shortcuts to success—he must sweat to earn the India colours!</speak>

whiteboard_commands.label: Madhav Mantri: 'Sweat to Earn India Colours'

sections.notes_content:
## Part 2: Family Influence Matrix

- **Mother**: Maternal patience, tennis-ball bowler, resilient reaction to injury.
- **Father**: Technical advice, cricketing discussions.
- **Uncle Madhav Mantri (former Indian test cricketer)**: Taught integrity; refused to give Sunil his India cap, stating that one must sweat to earn it.
key_takeaways: Mentorship shapes ethical and professional excellence
Sunil learned that merit and hard work surpass nepotism or entitlement

sections.title: Part 3: Speaking Skills: Asking and Answering Questions
sections.speech_ssml: <speak>Language is both written and spoken! <mark name='speak1'/> Practice asking clear, polite questions using who, what, where, and when. Notice how Sunil frames questions about fate and destiny with proper conversational cadence.</speak>
sections.notes_content:
## Part 3: Spoken English & Inquiry

- Wh- questions use falling intonation (*Where was the baby found?*).
- Yes/No questions use rising intonation (*Did Nan-kaka see the hole?*).
- Clear articulation of consonant blends.
key_takeaways: Master conversational cadence and interrogative intonation
Ask probing questions during oral examinations
Engage in interactive AI speech checks with Dr. Nova

exam_questions.question: Write an elaborate 10-mark essay detailing the autobiography 'My First Steps' by Sunil Gavaskar. Highlight the two defining childhood incidents, explain the grammatical features of the text, and discuss the moral lessons taught by Nan-kaka, his mother, and Madhav Mantri.
exam_questions.answer_key: 1. The Hospital Incident: Born July 10, 1949. Uncle Nan-kaka spotted the earlobe hole. Next day baby switched with a fisherwoman's baby; frantic search saved him. 2. Mother's Cricket Match: Hit on the nose by a tennis ball; bleeding nose; washed face and continued bowling, fostering resilience. 3. Grammatical Features: Rich use of compound words (earlobe, fisherwoman, eagle-eyed) and Simple Past Tense for completed actions and habits ('used to'/'would'). 4. Moral Lessons: Vigilance and observation (Nan-kaka), maternal dedication and sportsmanship (mother), and integrity with no shortcuts to success (Madhav Mantri).

course_description:
Course Description
Know first the basic terms like Autobiography, narrative voice, chronology, characters, conflict, and literary devices.
How to analyze Sunil Gavaskar's childhood extract 'My First Steps' and what are the reading rules to be followed. From initial comprehension to thematic depth – Deep discussion.
Explore the story within sections, across chapters, and through the broader historical context of Indian cricket.
Why identifying character traits and familial mentors is important to learn. A practical example is given using Narayan Masurekar (Nan-kaka).
How to understand the critical hospital incident where Sunil was nearly swapped at birth: What happened on July 10, 1949, how a tiny hole on his left earlobe saved his identity, and what would have happened if Nan-kaka had not looked closely – Which baby was he sleeping beside (the fisherwoman's baby) and Why?
Analyzing childhood cricket games with his mother in the gallery: What happened when a straight drive broke his mother's nose, how she reacted, and why her courage inspired him.
Uncle Madhav Mantri's pivotal life lesson: Why Sunil could not simply take India test pullovers from his uncle's wardrobe – 'Sweat to earn the India colours', there are no short-cuts to the top.
How to deal with unsporting childhood behavior: Walking away with the bat and ball when given out, the Ambaye and Mandrekar brothers' clever majority verdict appeals, and practical lessons on team spirit.
How and WHY are the two questions – We keep asking ourselves in this course throughout.
Why careful observation (eagle-eyed inspection) is better than passive acceptance.
How character perseverance achieves distinctions that short-cuts cannot.
Mastering Vocabulary Enrichment: Forming New Words – Compound Words in depth.
Deep discussion on the 3 types of compound words: Open compound words (car park, swimming pool), Hyphenated compound words (eagle-eyed, second-class), and Closed compound words (fisherwoman, staircase).
Which compound form is better and rules for hyphenation in compound nouns vs compound adjectives.
Mastering Grammar: The Simple Past Tense from fundamentals to advanced.
Regular verbs (add -ed) vs Irregular verbs (sleep -> slept, find -> found, bring -> brought).
How to form negative sentences using 'did not' + base verb (e.g. 'did not notice', not 'did not noticed').
How to form interrogative questions using 'Did' + subject + base verb.
Expressing habitual past actions using 'would' and 'used to'.
Study Skills: Note-Making Mastery from basics to advanced.
How to extract main points, hierarchical headings, subheadings, and indenting.
Using standard abbreviations (e.g., govt., b/w, dept., yr.) and numerical symbols to condense text for fast revision.
Synthesizing 1-mark, 2-mark, 5-mark, and 10-mark examination answers with complete textual evidence.
